Sunbit takes about a minute to apply and does not affect your credit score to check. The practice also works with CareCredit and Scratchpay. For ongoing treatment, a membership is usually cheaper: the monthly amount becomes credit that accumulates instead of expiring.
The comparisons people get stuck on.
or a neck lift: how do I know which?
A neck lift uses small incisions behind the ears and under the chin, and can last up to ten years. MyEllevate
places internal sutures through small punctures, and lasts around five. MyEllevate
suits earlier laxity; a neck lift reverses advanced sagging, wrinkling or fullness. MyEllevate
also needs only local anaesthetic, so you can drive yourself home.
Will a neck lift fix my jowls?
No, and it is the most common mix-up. Jowls sit low, so people assume neck work, but they originate in sagging facial tissue. A minimally invasive facelift is the procedure that reduces them.

Fillers are gel injectables that plump and smooth lines, acne scars and thin lips, lasting months to a couple of years by product and site. Implants are customised, biocompatible inserts that reshape the structure beneath and stay intact, so the contour is permanent. Filler changes the surface, an implant the frame.
How long does each result actually last?
The practice’s published figures: blepharoplasty 10–15 years or more; a neck lift up to ten; MyEllevate

around five; facial implants and buccal fat reduction permanent, though significant weight gain can return fullness to the cheek elsewhere. Injectables are months, not years: maintenance, not surgery.
Can I have more than one procedure at once?

Often, and frequently the better plan: a neck lift alongside a facelift or eyelid surgery means one recovery instead of two. What combines safely depends on your anatomy and time under anaesthetic, decided at the consultation.
Why do some rows say “at consultation” instead of a price?
Because the practice never published a figure for those, and we would rather show a gap than a guess. Genioplasty, fat transfer and facelift fees vary with the case, as the practice’s own pages say.

props.text: Eyelid surgery, upper or lower. The smallest operation on this list and, for most faces, the one that changes the most.
Upper or lower, as the practice's own price list quotes it
Three tissues, and the skin is only the first of them.
The practice describes the upper lid operation in one sentence: excess skin, muscle and fat, removed and repositioned. Most people come for the first. The last usually changes the most.
The fat behind the muscle, pushing forward as the tissue holding it back gives way. It is what a bag under the eye is made of.
Modern technique increasingly repositions this fat into the hollow beneath the eye rather than removing it. Removal is how a lid ends up hollow instead of rested.
A strip of the muscle that circles the eye, addressed where it contributes to the fold, through the same opening as the skin.
The layer nobody asks about, and why two lids with the same skin removed can settle differently.
The fold on the crease, on the lashes, or in marked cases in the outer field of vision. The layer everybody names first.
On the lower lid it punishes over-resection hardest: take too much and the lid pulls away from the eye.
The test is what happens when the brow is held where it used to sit.
Lift the tail of your brow with a fingertip. If that millimetre opens the eye, you need a brow lift, not this. If the eye stays heavy with the brow up, the weight is in the lid.
Which of these sound like you?
Upper lid skin that folds over the crease, or sits on the lashes
Bags or puffiness there the moment you wake, not only after a bad night
Hollowing beneath the eye that makes cheek and lid read as two structures
Eye makeup that no longer sits on the upper lid because there is nowhere flat for it

On the upper lid the incision sits in the natural crease and disappears once healed. Excess skin, muscle and fat are removed or repositioned through that one opening.
On the lower lid it goes just beneath the lash line, or inside the lid where only fat is being addressed, which leaves no external scar.

It is an outpatient operation of an hour or less, under local anaesthetic with sedation or a general where the work or the patient calls for it. The practice uses a long-acting local that can carry pain relief for forty to seventy two hours, so most patients need nothing stronger at home. A platelet rich plasma or platelet rich fibrin treatment can be added during the procedure to help the site heal.
A morning, a week of bruising, and a lid that keeps settling.

One to two hours if upper and lower lids are done together. Somebody else drives: sedation rules it out for twenty four hours.
Cold compresses and sleeping propped up shorten it considerably. Tenderness, watering, light sensitivity and some blurring from the ointment are all normal.
At around a week. Most of the healing happens inside the first fortnight and most people are back to normal activities within it.
Comfortable in company, then in photographs
Comfortable in company at ten days, in photographs at three weeks. The last swelling resolves over two to three months and the scar keeps fading past that.
The bruising week is at home, and it is a week.
By three weeks most people have stopped avoiding cameras.
Three different answers to "something about my eyes".
These are not three sizes of the same operation. One works above the eye, one on the lid, one on the surface of the skin, and it is common to need two. Each is quoted separately.

Five to ten days of social downtime
Dermal filler is a fourth conversation: it can soften a hollow under the eye at $800 a syringe, but it removes no skin and repositions no fat, so it does nothing for a heavy lid.
A lower lid gives back nothing that is taken from it in error.

Lower lids punish over-resection: take too much skin or fat and the lid pulls away from the eye, which is difficult to correct. The practice puts eyelid surgery at ten to fifteen years or more, and upper lid surgery is a once in a lifetime operation for most patients. You continue to age, but the tissue removed does not come back, though some choose to repeat it later for new sagging.

Occasionally, for upper lids only, where excess skin is documented to obstruct the visual field. That needs formal visual field testing and photographs. It is a question for your insurer, and most cases are cosmetic.
Can filler or laser do this instead?

They address different things. Filler can soften a hollow under the eye, laser can improve the texture of thin lid skin, and for early changes either may be enough. Neither removes excess skin or repositions fat.

You and Dr. Stone go through your concerns and goals. She takes a medical history, assesses your general health, and takes photographs and measurements to draw the plan against your own anatomy. You leave knowing whether this is the right procedure, and if not, which one is.
